title: How to Use an ABLE Account to Make Everyday Purchases

body_markdown:
For many people with disabilities, an[ABLE (Achieving a Better Life Experience) account](https://www.abletoday.org/overview) can be a great way to save, invest, and spend money. ABLE Accounts offer a number of benefits for those who are eligible, from being able to make everyday purchases without compromising eligibility for certain public benefits programs, like Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), to being able to invest in a tax-advantaged account and save for long-term expenses.


## **What is an ABLE Account?**


An ABLE account is a tax-advantaged savings account for people with qualifying disabilities. It's designed to let individuals save and spend money on disability-related needs without putting their public benefits at risk.


At a high level, here's what you should know:


- An[ABLE account](https://www.abletoday.org/overview) is owned by the person with the disability
- Money invested grows tax-free and withdrawals for qualifying expenses are also tax-free
- Up to $100,000 in the account is exempt from SSI's $2,000[countable asset limit](https://www.ssa.gov/ssi/spotlights/spot-resources.htm)
- Anyone can contribute: family members, friends, or the account holder themselves
- Annual contribution limits vary by year, and some contribution limits differ by state (e.g., life balance caps vary by state plan, ABLE to Work contributions vary by state of residence)


## How does someone enroll **in an ABLE Account** ?


The ABLE Act allows states to establish tax-advantaged programs for individuals with disabilities, similar to 529 college savings accounts or 401(k) retirement accounts. You are eligible to establish an ABLE account if you[have a qualifying disability and meet the ABLE Act](https://www.ablenrc.org/get-started/am-i-eligible/) ’[s age requirement](https://www.ablenrc.org/get-started/am-i-eligible/) . As of January 1, 2026, the age-of-onset threshold expanded from 26 to 46 years of age, so a person now qualifies if their disability began before age 46.[Most states have an ABLE program](https://www.ablenrc.org/select-a-state-program/) , but even if your state doesn’t have its own program, many ABLE programs allow out-of-state residents to open accounts.


ABLE accounts offer some similar features to typical bank accounts, but they are considered an[investment account, not a checking or savings account](https://www.ablenrc.org/get-started/how-do-i-manage-my-account/) . When you open an ABLE account, most programs will ask you to choose from a range of investment options that vary by risk, often including an FDIC-insured option. What’s valuable about ABLE accounts is that they allow individuals to build assets through savings and investments while also being able to withdraw and spend funds when they need to.


## **ABLE Account Eligibility: Who Qualifies?**


If you're helping a loved one decide whether an ABLE account is right for them, our guide to[ABLE Accounts Explained](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/blog/able-accounts-explained-a-financial-tool-for-loved-ones-with-disabilities) is a good starting point. According to the[ABLE National Resource Center](https://www.ablenrc.org/what-is-able/what-are-able-accounts/) , someone can qualify for an ABLE account in one of two ways:


- They are already receiving SSI or Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI).
- A licensed physician certifies that they have a physical or mental impairment causing marked and severe functional limitations.


In both cases, the disability must have begun before age 46, one of the[recent changes to ABLE accounts](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/blog/big-changes-coming-to-able-accounts-through-2027) that took effect in 2026. Eligibility is based on when the disability began, its onset, not the date of diagnosis.


## **How Much Money Can Be Contributed?**


The 2026 annual contribution limit is $20,000 and anyone can contribute. For account holders who are employed and not contributing to an employer retirement plan, the[ABLE-to-Work](https://www.ablenrc.org/able-to-work-act/) provision allows additional contributions, up to $15,650 in 2026 or their earnings (whichever is less), from their own earned income beyond the standard limit. Some states also offer a state income tax deduction for contributions, which varies by plan.


## How does spending **money from an ABLE Account** work?


True Link partners with several ABLE programs (see full list below) to provide a[True Link Visa®️ Prepaid Card](https://stableaccount.com/prepaid) to their participants. To use ABLE Account funds, the account holders and/or their Authorized Legal Representatives (ALRs) can move funds from the ABLE Account onto the True Link Visa Card and then use the Visa card to make purchases everywhere Visa debit cards are accepted.


Being able to spend money independently from an ABLE Account can also have a big impact on quality of life. The combination of fewer spending restrictions with ABLE Accounts and the ability to make purchases for themselves, can give individuals with disabilities more financial autonomy and personal freedoms than they’ve had before.


## **Keeping records** and what money can be used for


It's important that ABLE Account holders maintain good records of how they're using their funds in case they need to demonstrate that funds were used for qualified disability expenses (QDEs). If ABLE funds are used for non-qualified expenses, the earnings portion attributable to those non-qualified distributions may be included in taxable income and generally subject to an additional 10% federal tax. Fortunately, the IRS definition of a QDE is intentionally broad. An ABLE account can be used for a wide range of disability-related expenses. Some common QDEs include:


- **Basic Living Expenses:** Groceries, clothing, and personal care.
- **Housing:** Rent, mortgage payments, property taxes, and utilities.
- **Transportation:** Car payments, gas, repairs, and public transit.
- **Health and Wellness:** Co-pays, mental health services, and therapy not covered by insurance.
- **Education and Employment:** Tuition, books, and job coaching.


Expenses don't need to be medically necessary, and purchases are eligible if they help a person with disabilities maintain or improve health, independence, or quality of life. You can keep up with upcoming changes[here](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/blog/big-changes-coming-to-able-accounts-through-2027?_gl=1*1fga74*_up*MQ..&gclid=CjwKCAjwnZfPBhAGEiwAzg-VzC2iWEf8okavAOSqOABCH0S7ljclmX-AR0brCHKZoujXbJkI2uKu7BoC4KwQAvD_BwE&gbraid=0AAAAAB0m6mj33dfezPk6W0DYJLJGe_mah) .


True Link makes it easy[to keep track of these expenses](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/prepaid-card) in one place and pull records of purchases. Within the online platform, ABLE Account holders can upload receipts or leave notes about purchase details.


## **Managing spending as an Authorized Legal Representative**


If you’re an ALR who helps an individual with disabilities manage their funds, using a prepaid card like True Link’s can have additional benefits. The True Link platform provides electronic record-keeping of all transactions and can allow an ALR designated by the individual to see where and when purchases were made, as well as receive alerts on certain transactions.


And as an ALR, you can order a Visa card for yourself to make purchases for the beneficiary, a Visa card for the beneficiary, or both. True Link's platform can be used to set up separate balances and spending controls, so you can decide how and where funds can be used.

True Link Visa Cards for ABLE Account holders are just one of the ways[True Link](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/) supports people with disabilities; we are dedicated to providing life-changing financial solutions to this community. In fact, the Social Security Administration provides guidelines in the[Program Operations Manual System](https://secure.ssa.gov/apps10/poms.nsf/Help?readform) (POMS) for using[True Link Visa Cards](https://www.truelinkfinancial.com/prepaid-card) to make disbursements from special needs/supplemental needs trusts for beneficiaries who receive SSI.


For families supporting a loved one living with disabilities, managing the costs of care can prove challenging. If your loved one qualifies, an ABLE account can be a concrete step toward longer-term financial stability. The accounts are free to open, the tax advantages can be compelling, and the asset protection can matter a lot for anyone relying on means-tested benefits.
